extracted.intended_audience: fiction and memoir writers preparing a synopsis for agents or editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting a one- to two-page synopsis that conveys a novel's or memoir's complete narrative arc for agent/editor assessment. Focuses on content, voice/tense, structure, and what to include or omit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: industry document not sales copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis is an industry document that helps an agent or editor quickly assess your story's appeal and if it's worth them reading the entire manuscript. Don’t confuse the synopsis with sales copy or marketing description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write punchy marketing copy or attempt to entice readers; instead reveal the story plainly so an agent/editor can judge structure, character motivation, and problems. It must reveal the ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the synopsis short: one- or two-page synopsis—about 500–1000 words, single spaced—as a default. Anything up to two pages is usually acceptable; most agents/editors will not be interested in a synopsis longer than a few pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start short. If submission guidelines mandate a different length, follow them. Aim to include only what materially affects the protagonist and the ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Synopses should usually be written in third person, present tense (even if your novel is written in first person). For memoirists, first person is recommended, though first or third is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third-person present for fiction unless told otherwise; use first person for memoir if that better reflects the narrator's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal the entire narrative arc and the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis must convey the book's entire narrative arc: what happens, who changes, and it has to reveal the ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the central conflict is resolved and how the protagonist's internal and external situation has changed by the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with protagonist's mindset and inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the synopsis with your protagonist: describe their mindset and motivations at the opening, then explain what happens to change their situation (the inciting incident). Motivation is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear what drives the protagonist to act; this orients the reader to stakes and choices that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and cause-effect sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paragraph should ideally move the story forward with strong cause-effect storytelling, unfolding in exactly the same order as in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write events in manuscript order so an editor can follow the logic; emphasize causal links rather than listing events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include major turning points and genre 'formula' beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about your genre's formula, if there is one, and be sure to include all major turning points associated with that formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If genre expectations demand certain plot beats, include them so an agent can see you understand and deliver on those expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include characters who materially affect the protagonist's decisions or the meaning of events; any character that merits placement should have at least two to three mentions. If the ending wouldn't make sense without the character, they belong in the synopsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce characters when they enter the story or when they contribute to the story moving forward. Minor walk-on roles should be generic ('the waitress').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plotting weeds and unnecessary detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not get bogged down in minutiae (e.g., fight choreography, how many punches are thrown). Focus on outcomes (who wins/loses) and significance rather than blow-by-blow detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim scenes to their functional effect on plot and character; omit choreography and small procedural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include emotion and reaction, not just plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A good synopsis includes the characters' emotions and reactions to what's happening so it doesn't read like a mechanical account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance story advancement (incident) with color (reaction) and show resulting decisions: Incident + Reaction = Decision. This prevents 'synopsis speak'—a sterile listing of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding and historical context: establish only what's necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If your story requires substantial worldbuilding or historical context, open with a brief paragraph that establishes the rules or cultural facts that make motives and conflict sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invented terms unless central; prefer plain-language explanations so an agent/editor isn't burdened with deciphering vocabulary. Example: for Harry Potter, explain Muggles vs wizards as needed upfront.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sectioning and subheadings except when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis should start and end without breaks, sections, or subheadings. Exceptions: unique narrative structures (intertwining timelines) where signposts like 'Paris, 1893' may be helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present the synopsis as a cast list or segmented outline unless your book's structure makes that the clearest option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names and naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to the names of main characters; minor characters should be described generically. It's common to put a character's name in all caps on first mention so key figures are easy to spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long descriptors of minor characters; use names sparingly and purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't analyze or interpret themes
rubrics_metrics.description: A synopsis tells the story but does not attempt to explain the story's meaning or themes (e.g., 'this is the story of how many ordinary people...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid meta statements about the book's significance; show the events and let the reader infer themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commenting on story construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include commentary such as 'in the climax of the novel' or other notes about the book's structure; focus on the events themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the narrative straightforwardly rather than describing how it's built.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit backstory to what affects motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive character backstory unless it directly ties to a character's motivations and actions throughout the book; a phrase or two is usually enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include backstory that is necessary to understand why a character acts in certain ways during the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue sparingly and only when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid including dialogue in a synopsis; if you do include speech, it must be absolutely iconic or represent a linchpin moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer description of reaction and action over quoted lines unless the dialogue is indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pose rhetorical or unanswered questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A synopsis should not ask rhetorical questions or leave questions unanswered; the goal is to tell the story definitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about plot outcomes and character fates rather than implying them through questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice: lean, clean, energetic language
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents/editors are not expecting a work of art in the synopsis, but they respond to lean, clean, powerful language—energy and vitality matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise phrasing (example: 'At work, Elizabeth confronts Peter about his remarks' vs a wordy sentence). Avoid overwrought or poetic description; when necessary, 'tell' rather than 'show' for brevity.
